extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, reviewers, and educated readers interested in novels and biography
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative principles for judging novels (characterization, plot, style) and biographical compilations (selection, arrangement, tone). Emphasises appropriate style, authenticity of voice, and prudence in moral or factual judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of complex characters (avoid extravagant single features)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief seats ... are reserved for the few who have excelled in the difficult art of portraying characters in which no single feature is extravagantly overcharged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters of the highest rank should be portrayed with balanced, multifaceted traits rather than as caricatures dominated by one exaggerated feature; only lesser comic humours may justify extreme single-feature development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humours / monomania in characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost every one of her men and women has some one propensity developed to a morbid degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing a single dominant humour for a character can lead to monotonous individual talk, but a large variety of distinct humours across a cast can produce a lively and agreeable diversity; examples include groups of eccentrics whose opposing oddities create comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot construction: plausibility vs effectiveness for character exhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Her plots are rudely constructed and improbable, if we consider them in themselves. But they are admirably framed for the purpose of exhibiting striking groups of eccentric characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improbable or rudely constructed plots may be acceptable when they are deliberately designed to bring characters together to reveal contrasts and produce comic or dramatic effects (e.g., violating probability to assemble several character-types in one room).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and tonal suitability (comedy vs pathos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Madame D’Arblay was most successful in comedy, and indeed in comedy which bordered on farce. ... she might have attained equal distinction in the pathetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the author's natural strengths (comic farce, pathos, etc.) and value moments of 'natural tenderness' that reveal versatility; judge works by how well they achieve the intended tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: ease, clarity, and freedom from offensive faults
rubrics_metrics.description: When she wrote her letters ... her style was not indeed brilliant or energetic; but it was easy, clear, and free from all offensive faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple, perspicuous, and agreeable style is a positive quality for fiction of manners; clarity and naturalness often outweigh forced brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of stylistic model; avoid imitating unsuitable authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: In an evil hour the author of Evelina took the Rambler for her model. Phraseology which is proper in a disquisition ... may be quite out of place in a tale of fashionable life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not adopt stylistic models unsuited to their subject or voice (e.g., applying Johnsonian cadences to scenes of everyday life); imitation of inappropriate styles produces passages that jar with genre and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of authorial voice; avoid forced elevated diction
rubrics_metrics.description: She determined to throw it away, and to adopt a style in which she could attain excellence only by achieving an almost miraculous victory over nature and over habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forcing oneself into an elevated or foreign mode of expression (attempting to 'be' another great writer) often results in verbose or detestable passages; authenticity is preferable to strained excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse effects of foreign influence and exile on style
rubrics_metrics.description: After the publication of Camilla, Madame D’Arblay resided ten years at Paris. ... She brought back a style which we are really at a loss to describe. It is a sort of broken Johnsonese, a barbarous patois...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long immersion in another language or literary culture can corrupt an author's native style, producing hybridized, awkward, or affected diction that undermines the work regardless of the ideas expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of textual specimens to judge stylistic change
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only by means of specimens that we can enable our readers to judge how widely Madame D’Arblay’s three styles differed from each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare representative passages from different periods of an author's career to evaluate changes in style and determine whether such changes are improvements or degradations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical selection and arrangement: judgment and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: A great part ... consists of extracts from the letters and journals of Lord Byron; and it is difficult to speak too highly of the skill which has been shown in the selection and arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compilers and biographers should exercise tasteful judgment in selecting and arranging material (omit anecdotes that should be suppressed, conceal names where appropriate) and aim to present the subject with humanity while preserving informative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographer's tone: restraint, fairness, and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Moore never thrusts himself between Lord Byron and the public. With the strongest temptations to egotism, he has said no more about himself than the subject absolutely required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good biographer writes to vindicate or illuminate the subject without inserting excessive personal display; maintain fairness, modesty, and a primary focus on the subject rather than on the author/compiler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and quality of letters/journals as source materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The extracts from the journals and correspondence of Lord Byron are in the highest degree valuable ... The letters ... are among the best in our language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters and journals can be valuable not only for information but for their literary merit; when selecting, pay attention to epistolary quality (avoid pieces showing stiffness or awkward transitions) and to whether letters were meant for public reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical prudence: avoid pronouncing judgment without sufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: We will not pronounce any judgment, we cannot, even in our own minds, form any judgment, on a transaction which is so imperfectly known to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should withhold firm moral or factual judgments when the facts are imperfectly known; show forbearance and avoid contributing to rash public condemnation based on rumor or partial accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral tone in fiction: depict life while maintaining moral propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: A tale might be written in which both the fashionable and the vulgar life of London might be exhibited with great force, and with broad comic humour, and which yet should not contain a single line inconsistent with rigid morality, or even with virgin delicacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is possible and laudable to portray wide social experience vividly while preserving decorum and moral propriety; this balance vindicates the novelist's moral responsibility and can expand the genre's respectability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/genre importance: originality and precedent-setting merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Evelina was the first tale written by a woman, and purporting to be a picture of life and manners, that lived or deserved to live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works not only on immediate quality but on their innovation and influence—whether they establish precedents, vindicate marginalized authorship (e.g., women writing novels of manners), or open a 'fair and noble province of letters.'
